newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, PM welcome Chinese, Indian leaders.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, PM welcome Chinese, Indian leaders.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday put aside domestic woes to give a warm welcome to high-level visitors from India and China, which Moscow sees as potential partners in the post Cold War world.
Yeltsin told Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda that Moscow was committed to maintaining close relations with New Delhi which it considers to have a key role in Asia.
"We have been friends for many decades and we remain friends," Yeltsin told Deve Gowda. "India remains a stabilising force in its region."

Russian news agencies said on Monday that Yeltsin, who is completing a dramatic cabinet reshuffle aimed at boosting stalled economic reform, had postponed his traditional weekly meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to focus on talks with Deve Gowda and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.
On Tuesday, instead of meeting Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin met Deve Gowda and then Qian, who came to prepare a visit by Chinese President Ziang Zemin planned for late April.
Both leaders held separate talks with Chernomyrdin and Qian later met Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

Deve Gowda and Qian are visiting Moscow days after Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton "agreed to disagree" over NATO's plans to invite former Soviet bloc states to join the Western defence alliance at their meeting in the Finnish capital Helsinki.

Russian officials say NATO's commitment to expansion, despite Moscow's objections, marks the end of the honeymoon period between Russia and the West that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Russia is now looking for allies elsewhere. China and India, which also have strains in their relations with the West, are among the most highly prized partners.
Moscow has traditionally had close relations with India, which were especially strong in the 1960s and 1970s when New Delhi was involved in conflicts with China and U.S. ally Pakistan.

The weakness of post-Soviet Russia made special relations with it less attractive for India. But bilateral links have started improving lately as Russia has begun focusing more on relations with traditional partners to its south and east.

In contrast with India, Beijing and Moscow formed a strong alliance in the early 1950s which later degenerated into bitter rivalry for leadership of the world communist movement and led to border clashes in the late 1960s.
Relations have improved dramatically since a visit to Beijing by Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev in 1989.

After talks Qian said in a clear reference to NATO's expansion that the partnership between China and Russia, which leaves no room for any kind of military blocs, was the best way to ensure regional security.
"This partnership is a whole new security concept which drastically differs from the Cold War-era mentality," he told a joint news conference with Primakov.

Primakov specifically hailed a pact reducing forces along the border between China and the former Soviet Union due to be signed by Russia, China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan during Jiang's visit.
"After signing this pact we will be able to say that we created a model for maintaining stability for the whole Asian and Pacific region and not only for this region," he said.
Deve Gowda crowned his visit to Moscow by signing a number of accords on cooperation in different sectors and creating a better climate for bilateral economic relations.

He also told journalists after signing documents with Chernomyrdin that the two sides have managed to sort out financial problems that had stalled building on a nuclear power station in the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu. Deve Gowda gave no details and Russian officials declined to comment.
